body: A measurement assigns a value to a specified quantity using a method and a reference. A marked length standard, for example, permits comparisons at the scale of its intervals. Calibration establishes how readings relate to reference values under stated conditions.

Measurement results have uncertainty. Repeating a measurement can show how readings vary under the repeat conditions. Close agreement among repeated readings does not eliminate a bias. An instrument that gives the same reading each time can still disagree with a reference standard.
credit: Centauri Archive editorial draft, written with AI assistance
limitations: An instrument result needs its quantity definition, method, reference conditions and uncertainty. A photograph of an instrument does not establish a record's calibration.
purpose: Explain calibration and uncertainty as parts of a defensible measurement.
